The Taraba State Artisanal and Small-Scale Miners Association (ASMA) has uncovered abandoned mining pits, some reportedly reaching depths of 100 metres, in Mayo-Kam, Bali Local Government Area, raising fresh concerns about public safety and the enforcement of the state’s ban on illegal mining.
The association’s State Chairman, Emmanuel George, who led an inspection of the affected sites, warned that the abandoned excavations could cause further deaths if urgent measures were not taken to secure them.
The discovery comes barely two months after a mining pit collapsed in the same community on September 17, with more than 20 people feared trapped. The incident, which reportedly involved women and children, triggered rescue operations, with the police subsequently confirming the recovery of five bodies.
Mr George described the affected mining landscape as a “graveyard”, saying the depth and condition of the abandoned pits posed serious threats to farmers, residents and unsuspecting visitors.
The discovery is particularly concerning given the Taraba State Government’s earlier suspension of mining activities and deployment of security agencies to enforce the ban following growing concerns over illegal mining, insecurity and environmental degradation.
In August, the state government announced that its anti-illegal mining task force had arrested 50 suspected illegal miners and dispersed more than 500 others in Gantu, also in Bali Local Government Area.
The operation involved military personnel, officers of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, local vigilantes and hunters, who were deployed to secure mining locations and prevent illegal operators from returning.

The government also constituted an eight-member task force in September to intensify enforcement against illegal mining and protect the state’s mineral resources.
However, the discovery of the abandoned pits raises questions about the effectiveness of these enforcement measures, particularly the monitoring, closure and rehabilitation of mining sites after illegal operators are dislodged.
The inspection team included federal mines officers, representatives of the mobile court and members of the Taraba State Mining Taskforce.
Mr George said the association would forward its findings to Governor Agbu Kefas for urgent intervention, particularly to address the exposed pits and other environmental hazards threatening communities around the mining locations.
He also confirmed the arrest of several suspects allegedly found hiding at the site, adding that they had been handed over to the appropriate authorities for investigation and possible prosecution.
The arrests, he said, formed part of ongoing efforts to curb illegal mining and strengthen regulatory enforcement in the state.
At the Gidan-Boss mining site, Mr George commended security operatives for maintaining order but dismissed allegations that they were using abandoned crushing machines for personal gain or tampering with mineral deposits.
According to him, an inspection of the equipment established that none of the crushing machines was operational and that the mineral deposits remained intact, contrary to allegations circulating about the activities of security personnel.
He appealed to local mining operators to remain calm, saying Governor Kefas had directed the evacuation of abandoned crushing equipment as part of the government’s broader plan to sanitise, regulate and formalise mining operations.
Mr George urged miners, community leaders and other stakeholders to support the government’s regulatory efforts, stressing that responsible mining practices were necessary to prevent avoidable deaths, curb environmental degradation and protect mineral resources.
He added that improved regulation of the sector could create sustainable employment opportunities for young people in Taraba.
The latest discovery highlights the challenges confronting the state government in its efforts to end illegal mining, particularly in remote communities where abandoned excavations remain potential hazards long after mining operations have stopped.
It also raises questions about who will take responsibility for securing and rehabilitating the pits, whether adequate funds have been provided for the exercise and what measures are being taken to prevent another mining disaster in Mayo-Kam.
